beats.intro: Chapter ten. [[sub]]A company does not compete in a vacuum. This chapter shows how to define an industry, measure it, and judge a company's position within it.
beats.classification: First, define the industry. [[old]]Early schemes, such as SIC, NACE and ISIC, grouped companies by how they produce things, and were slow to change. [[new]]Today analysts use commercial schemes: GICS, ICB and TRBC. They group companies by what they sell, are global, and are updated at least annually. [[tax]]They are strict hierarchies. Each company sits in exactly one lowest-level group, which then sets its sector. [[limit]]That is tidy, but a company selling very different products still gets a single label. [[cyc]]Analysts also group by sensitivity to the business cycle. Cyclical sectors, such as financials, materials, discretionary and industrials, move with the economy. Defensive sectors, such as staples, healthcare and utilities, hold up better.
beats.growth: Next, survey the industry. [[size]]Estimate its size: total annual sales. [[rate]]Measure its growth, and compare it with the economy. [[early]]Early on, the industry grows far faster than GDP. [[mature]]Later, growth settles close to GDP: a sign of maturity. [[note]]Also look at profitability, and at whether sales swing with the business cycle. Companies at different life-cycle stages in the same industry can have very different profiles.
beats.concentration: Who holds the market? [[a]]Take four companies with shares of forty, thirty, twenty and ten percent. [[sq]]The Herfindahl-Hirschman Index adds up the squares of the shares: sixteen hundred, plus nine hundred, plus four hundred, plus one hundred, which is three thousand. [[frag]]Ten companies with ten percent each give one thousand. [[note]]A higher index means a more concentrated industry. That usually means less intense rivalry, and the potential for higher profitability. Track shares over time, because trends matter as much as levels.
beats.forces: Porter's five forces explain why profitability differs between industries. Take airlines, as an illustration. [[rival]]Rivalry among existing competitors: high. Capacity is expensive, fares are easy to compare. [[entr]]Threat of new entrants: medium. [[subs]]Threat of substitutes: medium. Think of rail, or video calls. [[buy]]Buyer power: high. Customers compare prices online. [[sup]]Supplier power: high. Aircraft makers, fuel sellers, and labor unions. [[sum]]Add it up, and the industry structure points to low profitability, however good any single airline may be.
beats.pestle: Five forces describe structure. PESTLE describes what is changing around it. [[p]]Political: trade policy, subsidies, taxes. [[e]]Economic: growth, interest rates, inflation. [[s]]Social: demographics and tastes. [[t]]Technological: automation, digital channels. [[l]]Legal: regulation and competition law. [[env]]Environmental: climate rules, packaging taxes. [[note]]PESTLE helps identify themes that change an industry's growth rate and market shares.
beats.strategy: Finally, judge the company's strategy. [[cost]]Cost leadership competes on a low price, which suits price-sensitive customers with low switching costs. It needs scale and fixed-cost discipline. [[diff]]Differentiation competes on something customers value, such as luxury, performance, or brand, and allows higher prices. [[test]]Then test the strategy. Does it defend against the five forces? Does it fit the external trends from PESTLE? And does the company have the resources and capabilities to carry it out?
beats.wrap: Four things to keep. [[w1]]Define the industry with a classification scheme, and know its limits. [[w2]]Measure industry size, growth, profitability, and market share trends. Concentration is the sum of squared shares. [[w3]]Five forces assess structure. PESTLE assesses outside influences. [[w4]]A good strategy defends against the forces, fits the trends, and can be executed.
